newsitem.title: USA: D.C. panel orders $85.6 mln in D.C. budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: D.C. panel orders $85.6 mln in D.C. budget cuts.

text.p: The nation's capital was ordered on Friday to slash its fiscal 1997 budget by $85.6 million to avoid exceeding spending limits set by Congress.
The cuts were ordered by the congressionally appointed District of Columbia financial control board, which is trying to improve the city's poor financial health, and had been widely expected.
The five-member panel, however, did not spell out how many jobs Mayor Marion Barry and agency officials would have to cut to achieve those savings.
"We did not identify the number of reductions. (But) we fully anticipate some reductions must be made," control board chairman Andrew Brimmer told a public meeting.
Published reports had said the control board would slash 1,000 jobs but Brimmer said he had never mentioned a number.
The control board was appointed in 1995 to oversee the District's finances.

For most of its history, the 10-square mile District has been controlled by the federal government and Congress. But in 1974, Congress granted the District financial independence and the right to vote for a mayor and city council.
Now the city is in dire financial straits with a bloated bureaucracy, crumbling school system and unreliable municipal services.

The control board has called on the federal government to assume some of the financial burden; essentially, to take on the role that a state plays to other American cities. President Clinton has promised to try to resolve the problem.

Brimmer said at Friday's meeting that the board carefully considered all recommendations by the mayor, chief financial officer Anthony Williams and the D.C. council. "We selected a number of items from each set of proposals," he said.

He said the city's highest priorities were public schools, public safety and public works. "While reductions were made in these areas, the cuts were proportionally less than the overall average decrease," Brimmer said.
Control board Vice Chairman Stephen Harlan warned that the city is only three months into the current fiscal year and "additional adjustments" in the budget may be needed.

The control board on Friday outlined several upcoming cuts, including a $16.2 million reduction in the annual budget of the University of the District of Columbia and $8 million in reductions in summer youth and youth violence programmes.
The control board also ordered the city to cut $9 million in administrative services, $1 million in subsidies to the D.C. General Hospital, and $8 million in spending for corrections services.
The panel ordered the city to save $5.4 million by reducing overtime payments to D.C. workers and to cut police department full-time employee costs by $1.4 million.
